sp.p: O, for the love of laughter, let him fetch his drum; he says he has a stratagem for’t. When your lordship sees the bottom of his success in’t, and to what metal this counterfeit lump of ore will be melted, if you give him not John Drum’s entertainment, your inclining cannot be removed. Here he comes.

sp.speaker: FIRST LORD
sp.p: O, for the love of laughter, hinder not the honour of his design: let him fetch off his drum in any hand.

sp.speaker: BERTRAM
sp.p: How now, monsieur! This drum sticks sorely in your disposition.

sp.speaker: SECOND LORD
sp.p: A pox on ’t; let it go; ’tis but a drum.

sp.speaker: PAROLLES
sp.p: But a drum! Is’t but a drum? A drum so lost! There was excellent command, to charge in with our horse upon our own wings, and to rend our own soldiers.

sp.speaker: SECOND LORD
sp.p: That was not to be blam’d in the command of the service; it was a disaster of war that Caesar himself could not have prevented, if he had been there to command.

sp.speaker: BERTRAM
sp.p: Well, we cannot greatly condemn our success: some dishonour we had in the loss of that drum, but it is not to be recovered.

sp.speaker: PAROLLES
sp.p: It might have been recovered.

sp.speaker: BERTRAM
sp.p: It might, but it is not now.

sp.speaker: PAROLLES
sp.p: It is to be recovered. But that the merit of service is seldom attributed to the true and exact performer, I would have that drum or another, or hic jacet.

sp.speaker: BERTRAM
sp.p: Why, if you have a stomach, to’t, monsieur, if you think your mystery in stratagem can bring this instrument of honour again into his native quarter, be magnanimous in the enterprise, and go on; I will grace the attempt for a worthy exploit; if you speed well in it, the duke shall both speak of it and extend to you what further becomes his greatness, even to the utmost syllable of your worthiness.

sp.speaker: PAROLLES
sp.p: By the hand of a soldier, I will undertake it.

sp.speaker: BERTRAM
sp.p: But you must not now slumber in it.

sp.speaker: PAROLLES
sp.p: I’ll about it this evening; and I will presently pen down my dilemmas, encourage myself in my certainty, put myself into my mortal preparation; and by midnight look to hear further from me.

sp.speaker: BERTRAM
sp.p: May I be bold to acquaint his grace you are gone about it?

sp.speaker: PAROLLES
sp.p: I know not what the success will be, my lord, but the attempt I vow.

sp.speaker: BERTRAM
sp.p: I know th’art valiant; and to the possibility of thy soldiership, will subscribe for thee. Farewell.

sp.speaker: PAROLLES
sp.p: I love not many words.

sp.speaker: FIRST LORD
sp.p: No more than a fish loves water. Is not this a strange fellow, my lord, that so confidently seems to undertake this business, which he knows is not to be done; damns himself to do, and dares better be damn’d than to do’t.

sp.speaker: SECOND LORD
sp.p: You do not know him, my lord, as we do; certain it is that he will steal himself into a man’s favour, and for a week escape a great deal of discoveries, but when you find him out, you have him ever after.

sp.speaker: BERTRAM
sp.p: Why, do you think he will make no deed at all of this, that so seriously he does address himself unto?

sp.speaker: FIRST LORD
sp.p: None in the world; but return with an invention, and clap upon you two or three probable lies; but we have almost embossed him; you shall see his fall tonight; for indeed he is not for your lordship’s respect.

sp.speaker: SECOND LORD
sp.p: We’ll make you some sport with the fox ere we case him. He was first smok’d by the old Lord Lafew; when his disguise and he is parted, tell me what a sprat you shall find him; which you shall see this very night.

sp.speaker: FIRST LORD
sp.p: I must go look my twigs. He shall be caught.

sp.speaker: BERTRAM
sp.p: Your brother, he shall go along with me.

sp.speaker: FIRST LORD
sp.p: As’t please your lordship. I’ll leave you.

lg.l: Now will I lead you to the house, and show you
The lass I spoke of.

sp.speaker: SECOND LORD
sp.p: But you say she’s honest.

lg.l: That’s all the fault. I spoke with her but once,
And found her wondrous cold, but I sent to her
By this same coxcomb that we have i’ the wind
Tokens and letters which she did re-send,
And this is all I have done. She’s a fair creature;
Will you go see her?

sp.speaker: SECOND LORD
sp.p: With all my heart, my lord.

div.head: SCENE VII. Florence. A room in the Widow’s house.

lg.l: If you misdoubt me that I am not she,
I know not how I shall assure you further,
But I shall lose the grounds I work upon.
Though my estate be fall’n, I was well born,
Nothing acquainted with these businesses,
And would not put my reputation now
In any staining act.
Nor would I wish you.
First give me trust, the count he is my husband,
And what to your sworn counsel I have spoken
Is so from word to word; and then you cannot,
By the good aid that I of you shall borrow,
Err in bestowing it.
I should believe you,
For you have show’d me that which well approves
Y’are great in fortune.
Take this purse of gold,
And let me buy your friendly help thus far,
Which I will over-pay, and pay again
When I have found it. The count he woos your daughter
Lays down his wanton siege before her beauty,
Resolv’d to carry her; let her in fine consent,
As we’ll direct her how ’tis best to bear it.
Now his important blood will naught deny
That she’ll demand; a ring the county wears,
That downward hath succeeded in his house
From son to son, some four or five descents
Since the first father wore it. This ring he holds
In most rich choice; yet, in his idle fire,
To buy his will, it would not seem too dear,
Howe’er repented after.
Now I see
The bottom of your purpose.
You see it lawful then; it is no more
But that your daughter, ere she seems as won,
Desires this ring; appoints him an encounter;
In fine, delivers me to fill the time,
Herself most chastely absent. After,
To marry her, I’ll add three thousand crowns
To what is pass’d already.
I have yielded.
Instruct my daughter how she shall persever,
That time and place with this deceit so lawful
May prove coherent. Every night he comes
With musics of all sorts, and songs compos’d
To her unworthiness: it nothing steads us
To chide him from our eaves; for he persists
As if his life lay on ’t.
Why then tonight
Let us assay our plot; which, if it speed,
Is wicked meaning in a lawful deed,
And lawful meaning in a lawful act,
Where both not sin, and yet a sinful fact.
But let’s about it.

div.head: ACT IV
SCENE I. Without the Florentine camp.
div.stage: Enter first Lord with five or six Soldiers in ambush.

sp.speaker: FIRST LORD
sp.p: He can come no other way but by this hedge-corner. When you sally upon him, speak what terrible language you will; though you understand it not yourselves, no matter; for we must not seem to understand him, unless someone among us, whom we must produce for an interpreter.

sp.speaker: FIRST SOLDIER
sp.p: Good captain, let me be th’ interpreter.

sp.speaker: FIRST LORD
sp.p: Art not acquainted with him? Knows he not thy voice?

sp.speaker: FIRST SOLDIER
sp.p: No sir, I warrant you.

sp.speaker: FIRST LORD
sp.p: But what linsey-woolsey has thou to speak to us again?

sp.speaker: FIRST SOLDIER
sp.p: E’en such as you speak to me.

sp.speaker: FIRST LORD
sp.p: He must think us some band of strangers i’ the adversary’s entertainment. Now he hath a smack of all neighbouring languages, therefore we must every one be a man of his own fancy; not to know what we speak one to another, so we seem to know, is to know straight our purpose: choughs’ language, gabble enough, and good enough. As for you, interpreter, you must seem very politic. But couch, ho! Here he comes; to beguile two hours in a sleep, and then to return and swear the lies he forges.

sp.speaker: PAROLLES
sp.p: Ten o’clock. Within these three hours ’twill be time enough to go home. What shall I say I have done? It must be a very plausive invention that carries it. They begin to smoke me, and disgraces have of late knock’d too often at my door. I find my tongue is too foolhardy, but my heart hath the fear of Mars before it, and of his creatures, not daring the reports of my tongue.

sp.speaker: FIRST LORD
sp.p: Aside. This is the first truth that e’er thine own tongue was guilty of.

sp.speaker: PAROLLES
sp.p: What the devil should move me to undertake the recovery of this drum, being not ignorant of the impossibility, and knowing I had no such purpose? I must give myself some hurts, and say I got them in exploit; yet slight ones will not carry it. They will say “Came you off with so little?” and great ones I dare not give. Wherefore, what’s the instance? Tongue, I must put you into a butter-woman’s mouth, and buy myself another of Bajazet’s mule, if you prattle me into these perils.

sp.speaker: FIRST LORD
sp.p: Aside. Is it possible he should know what he is, and be that he is?

sp.speaker: PAROLLES
sp.p: I would the cutting of my garments would serve the turn, or the breaking of my Spanish sword.

sp.speaker: FIRST LORD
sp.p: Aside. We cannot afford you so.

sp.speaker: PAROLLES
sp.p: Or the baring of my beard, and to say it was in stratagem.

sp.speaker: FIRST LORD
sp.p: Aside. ’Twould not do.

sp.speaker: PAROLLES
sp.p: Or to drown my clothes, and say I was stripped.

sp.speaker: FIRST LORD
sp.p: Aside. Hardly serve.

sp.speaker: PAROLLES
sp.p: Though I swore I leap’d from the window of the citadel,—

sp.speaker: FIRST LORD
sp.p: Aside. How deep?

sp.speaker: PAROLLES
sp.p: Thirty fathom.

sp.speaker: FIRST LORD
sp.p: Aside. Three great oaths would scarce make that be believed.

sp.speaker: PAROLLES
sp.p: I would I had any drum of the enemy’s; I would swear I recover’d it.

sp.speaker: FIRST LORD
sp.p: Aside. You shall hear one anon.

sp.speaker: PAROLLES
sp.p: A drum now of the enemy’s!

p.emph: Cargo, cargo, cargo, villianda par corbo, cargo.

sp.speaker: PAROLLES
sp.p: O, ransom, ransom! Do not hide mine eyes.

lg.l: I know you are the Muskos’ regiment,
And I shall lose my life for want of language.
If there be here German, or Dane, Low Dutch,
Italian, or French, let him speak to me,
I’ll discover that which shall undo the Florentine.

sp.speaker: FIRST SOLDIER
sp.p: Boskos vauvado. I understand thee, and can speak thy tongue. Kerelybonto. Sir, Betake thee to thy faith, for seventeen poniards are at thy bosom.

sp.speaker: PAROLLES
sp.p: O!

lg.l: O, pray, pray, pray!
The General is content to spare thee yet;
And, hoodwink’d as thou art, will lead thee on
To gather from thee. Haply thou mayst inform
Something to save thy life.
O, let me live,
And all the secrets of our camp I’ll show,
Their force, their purposes; nay, I’ll speak that
Which you will wonder at.

sp.speaker: FIRST SOLDIER
sp.p: But wilt thou faithfully?

sp.speaker: PAROLLES
sp.p: If I do not, damn me.

lg.l: Come on; thou art granted space.
Go tell the Count Rossillon and my brother
We have caught the woodcock, and will keep him muffled
Till we do hear from them.

sp.speaker: SECOND SOLDIER
sp.p: Captain, I will.

lg.l: ’A will betray us all unto ourselves;
Inform on that.

sp.speaker: SECOND SOLDIER
sp.p: So I will, sir.

sp.speaker: FIRST LORD
sp.p: Till then I’ll keep him dark, and safely lock’d.

div.head: SCENE II. Florence. A room in the Widow’s house.

sp.speaker: BERTRAM
sp.p: They told me that your name was Fontybell.

sp.speaker: DIANA
sp.p: No, my good lord, Diana.

lg.l: Titled goddess;
And worth it, with addition! But, fair soul,
In your fine frame hath love no quality?
If the quick fire of youth light not your mind,
You are no maiden but a monument;
When you are dead, you should be such a one
As you are now; for you are cold and stern,
And now you should be as your mother was
When your sweet self was got.

sp.speaker: DIANA
sp.p: She then was honest.

sp.speaker: BERTRAM
sp.p: So should you be.

lg.l: No.
My mother did but duty; such, my lord,
As you owe to your wife.
No more a’ that!
I pr’ythee do not strive against my vows;
I was compell’d to her; but I love thee
By love’s own sweet constraint, and will for ever
Do thee all rights of service.
Ay, so you serve us
Till we serve you; but when you have our roses,
You barely leave our thorns to prick ourselves,
And mock us with our bareness.

sp.speaker: BERTRAM
sp.p: How have I sworn?

lg.l: ’Tis not the many oaths that makes the truth,
But the plain single vow that is vow’d true.
What is not holy, that we swear not by,
But take the highest to witness: then, pray you, tell me,
If I should swear by Jove’s great attributes
I lov’d you dearly, would you believe my oaths
When I did love you ill? This has no holding,
To swear by him whom I protest to love
That I will work against him. Therefore your oaths
Are words and poor conditions; but unseal’d,—
At least in my opinion.
Change it, change it.
Be not so holy-cruel. Love is holy;
And my integrity ne’er knew the crafts
That you do charge men with. Stand no more off,
But give thyself unto my sick desires,
Who then recovers. Say thou art mine, and ever
My love as it begins shall so persever.
I see that men make hopes in such a case,
That we’ll forsake ourselves. Give me that ring.
I’ll lend it thee, my dear, but have no power
To give it from me.

sp.speaker: DIANA
sp.p: Will you not, my lord?

lg.l: It is an honour ’longing to our house,
Bequeathed down from many ancestors,
Which were the greatest obloquy i’ the world
In me to lose.
Mine honour’s such a ring;
My chastity’s the jewel of our house,
Bequeathed down from many ancestors,
Which were the greatest obloquy i’ the world
In me to lose. Thus your own proper wisdom
Brings in the champion honour on my part
Against your vain assault.
Here, take my ring;
My house, mine honour, yea, my life be thine,
And I’ll be bid by thee.
When midnight comes, knock at my chamber window;
I’ll order take my mother shall not hear.
Now will I charge you in the band of truth,
When you have conquer’d my yet maiden-bed,
Remain there but an hour, nor speak to me.
My reasons are most strong; and you shall know them
When back again this ring shall be deliver’d;
And on your finger in the night, I’ll put
Another ring, that what in time proceeds
May token to the future our past deeds.
Adieu till then; then fail not. You have won
A wife of me, though there my hope be done.

sp.speaker: BERTRAM
sp.p: A heaven on earth I have won by wooing thee.

lg.l: For which live long to thank both heaven and me!
You may so in the end.
My mother told me just how he would woo,
As if she sat in’s heart. She says all men
Have the like oaths. He had sworn to marry me
When his wife’s dead; therefore I’ll lie with him
When I am buried. Since Frenchmen are so braid,
Marry that will, I live and die a maid.
Only, in this disguise, I think’t no sin
To cozen him that would unjustly win.

div.head: SCENE III. The Florentine camp.
div.stage: Enter the two French Lords and two or three Soldiers.

sp.speaker: FIRST LORD
sp.p: You have not given him his mother’s letter?

sp.speaker: SECOND LORD
sp.p: I have deliv’red it an hour since; there is something in’t that stings his nature; for on the reading it, he chang’d almost into another man.

sp.speaker: FIRST LORD
sp.p: He has much worthy blame laid upon him for shaking off so good a wife and so sweet a lady.

sp.speaker: SECOND LORD
sp.p: Especially he hath incurred the everlasting displeasure of the king, who had even tun’d his bounty to sing happiness to him. I will tell you a thing, but you shall let it dwell darkly with you.

sp.speaker: FIRST LORD
sp.p: When you have spoken it, ’tis dead, and I am the grave of it.

sp.speaker: SECOND LORD
sp.p: He hath perverted a young gentlewoman here in Florence, of a most chaste renown, and this night he fleshes his will in the spoil of her honour; he hath given her his monumental ring, and thinks himself made in the unchaste composition.

sp.speaker: FIRST LORD
sp.p: Now, God delay our rebellion! As we are ourselves, what things are we!

sp.speaker: SECOND LORD
sp.p: Merely our own traitors. And as in the common course of all treasons, we still see them reveal themselves till they attain to their abhorr’d ends; so he that in this action contrives against his own nobility, in his proper stream, o’erflows himself.

sp.speaker: FIRST LORD
sp.p: Is it not meant damnable in us to be trumpeters of our unlawful intents? We shall not then have his company tonight?

sp.speaker: SECOND LORD
sp.p: Not till after midnight; for he is dieted to his hour.

sp.speaker: FIRST LORD
sp.p: That approaches apace. I would gladly have him see his company anatomized, that he might take a measure of his own judgments, wherein so curiously he had set this counterfeit.

sp.speaker: SECOND LORD
sp.p: We will not meddle with him till he come; for his presence must be the whip of the other.

sp.speaker: FIRST LORD
sp.p: In the meantime, what hear you of these wars?

sp.speaker: SECOND LORD
sp.p: I hear there is an overture of peace.

sp.speaker: FIRST LORD
sp.p: Nay, I assure you, a peace concluded.

sp.speaker: SECOND LORD
sp.p: What will Count Rossillon do then? Will he travel higher, or return again into France?

sp.speaker: FIRST LORD
sp.p: I perceive by this demand, you are not altogether of his council.

sp.speaker: SECOND LORD
sp.p: Let it be forbid, sir! So should I be a great deal of his act.

sp.speaker: FIRST LORD
sp.p: Sir, his wife some two months since fled from his house. Her pretence is a pilgrimage to Saint Jaques le Grand; which holy undertaking with most austere sanctimony she accomplished; and there residing, the tenderness of her nature became as a prey to her grief; in fine, made a groan of her last breath, and now she sings in heaven.

sp.speaker: SECOND LORD
sp.p: How is this justified?

sp.speaker: FIRST LORD
sp.p: The stronger part of it by her own letters, which makes her story true, even to the point of her death. Her death itself, which could not be her office to say is come, was faithfully confirm’d by the rector of the place.

sp.speaker: SECOND LORD
sp.p: Hath the count all this intelligence?

sp.speaker: FIRST LORD
sp.p: Ay, and the particular confirmations, point from point, to the full arming of the verity.

sp.speaker: SECOND LORD
sp.p: I am heartily sorry that he’ll be glad of this.

sp.speaker: FIRST LORD
sp.p: How mightily sometimes we make us comforts of our losses!

sp.speaker: SECOND LORD
sp.p: And how mightily some other times we drown our gain in tears! The great dignity that his valour hath here acquir’d for him shall at home be encountered with a shame as ample.

sp.speaker: FIRST LORD
sp.p: The web of our life is of a mingled yarn, good and ill together; our virtues would be proud if our faults whipped them not; and our crimes would despair if they were not cherish’d by our virtues.

sp.speaker: MESSENGER
sp.p: He met the duke in the street, sir; of whom he hath taken a solemn leave: his lordship will next morning for France. The duke hath offered him letters of commendations to the king.

sp.speaker: SECOND LORD
sp.p: They shall be no more than needful there, if they were more than they can commend.

sp.speaker: FIRST LORD
sp.p: They cannot be too sweet for the king’s tartness. Here’s his lordship now. How now, my lord, is’t not after midnight?

sp.speaker: BERTRAM
sp.p: I have tonight despatch’d sixteen businesses, a month’s length apiece; by an abstract of success: I have congied with the duke, done my adieu with his nearest; buried a wife, mourn’d for her, writ to my lady mother I am returning, entertained my convoy, and between these main parcels of despatch effected many nicer needs: the last was the greatest, but that I have not ended yet.

sp.speaker: SECOND LORD
sp.p: If the business be of any difficulty and this morning your departure hence, it requires haste of your lordship.

sp.speaker: BERTRAM
sp.p: I mean the business is not ended, as fearing to hear of it hereafter. But shall we have this dialogue between the Fool and the Soldier? Come, bring forth this counterfeit module has deceiv’d me like a double-meaning prophesier.

sp.speaker: SECOND LORD
sp.p: Bring him forth.

div.p: Has sat i’ the stocks all night, poor gallant knave.

sp.speaker: BERTRAM
sp.p: No matter; his heels have deserv’d it, in usurping his spurs so long. How does he carry himself?

sp.speaker: FIRST LORD
sp.p: I have told your lordship already; the stocks carry him. But to answer you as you would be understood: he weeps like a wench that had shed her milk; he hath confessed himself to Morgan, whom he supposes to be a friar, from the time of his remembrance to this very instant disaster of his setting i’ the stocks. And what think you he hath confessed?

sp.speaker: BERTRAM
sp.p: Nothing of me, has he?

sp.speaker: SECOND LORD
sp.p: His confession is taken, and it shall be read to his face; if your lordship be in’t, as I believe you are, you must have the patience to hear it.

sp.speaker: BERTRAM
sp.p: A plague upon him! muffled! he can say nothing of me; hush, hush!

sp.speaker: FIRST LORD
sp.p: Hoodman comes! Portotartarossa.

sp.speaker: FIRST SOLDIER
sp.p: He calls for the tortures. What will you say without ’em?

sp.speaker: PAROLLES
sp.p: I will confess what I know without constraint. If ye pinch me like a pasty I can say no more.

sp.speaker: FIRST SOLDIER
sp.p: You are a merciful general. Our general bids you answer to what I shall ask you out of a note.

sp.speaker: PAROLLES
sp.p: And truly, as I hope to live.

sp.speaker: FIRST SOLDIER
sp.p: ‘First demand of him how many horse the duke is strong.’ What say you to that?

sp.speaker: PAROLLES
sp.p: Five or six thousand; but very weak and unserviceable: the troops are all scattered, and the commanders very poor rogues, upon my reputation and credit, and as I hope to live.

sp.speaker: FIRST SOLDIER
sp.p: Shall I set down your answer so?

sp.speaker: PAROLLES
sp.p: Do. I’ll take the sacrament on ’t, how and which way you will.

sp.speaker: BERTRAM
sp.p: All’s one to him. What a past-saving slave is this!

sp.speaker: FIRST LORD
sp.p: You are deceived, my lord; this is Monsieur Parolles, the gallant militarist (that was his own phrase), that had the whole theoric of war in the knot of his scarf, and the practice in the chape of his dagger.

sp.speaker: SECOND LORD
sp.p: I will never trust a man again for keeping his sword clean, nor believe he can have everything in him by wearing his apparel neatly.

sp.speaker: FIRST SOLDIER
sp.p: Well, that’s set down.

sp.speaker: PAROLLES
sp.p: ‘Five or six thousand horse’ I said—I will say true—or thereabouts, set down,—for I’ll speak truth.

sp.speaker: FIRST LORD
sp.p: He’s very near the truth in this.

sp.speaker: BERTRAM
sp.p: But I con him no thanks for’t in the nature he delivers it.

sp.speaker: PAROLLES
sp.p: Poor rogues, I pray you say.

sp.speaker: FIRST SOLDIER
sp.p: Well, that’s set down.

sp.speaker: PAROLLES
sp.p: I humbly thank you, sir; a truth’s a truth, the rogues are marvellous poor.

sp.speaker: FIRST SOLDIER
sp.p: ‘Demand of him of what strength they are a-foot.’ What say you to that?

sp.speaker: PAROLLES
sp.p: By my troth, sir, if I were to live this present hour, I will tell true. Let me see: Spurio, a hundred and fifty, Sebastian, so many; Corambus, so many; Jaques, so many; Guiltian, Cosmo, Lodowick, and Gratii, two hundred fifty each; mine own company, Chitopher, Vaumond, Bentii, two hundred fifty each: so that the muster-file, rotten and sound, upon my life, amounts not to fifteen thousand poll; half of the which dare not shake the snow from off their cassocks lest they shake themselves to pieces.

sp.speaker: BERTRAM
sp.p: What shall be done to him?

sp.speaker: FIRST LORD
sp.p: Nothing, but let him have thanks. Demand of him my condition, and what credit I have with the duke.

sp.speaker: FIRST SOLDIER
sp.p: Well, that’s set down. ‘You shall demand of him whether one Captain Dumaine be i’ the camp, a Frenchman; what his reputation is with the duke, what his valour, honesty and expertness in wars; or whether he thinks it were not possible with well-weighing sums of gold to corrupt him to a revolt.’ What say you to this? What do you know of it?

sp.speaker: PAROLLES
sp.p: I beseech you, let me answer to the particular of the inter’gatories. Demand them singly.

sp.speaker: FIRST SOLDIER
sp.p: Do you know this Captain Dumaine?

sp.speaker: PAROLLES
sp.p: I know him: he was a botcher’s ’prentice in Paris, from whence he was whipped for getting the shrieve’s fool with child, a dumb innocent that could not say him nay.

div.stage: First Lord lifts up his hand in anger.

sp.speaker: BERTRAM
sp.p: Nay, by your leave, hold your hands; though I know his brains are forfeit to the next tile that falls.

sp.speaker: FIRST SOLDIER
sp.p: Well, is this captain in the Duke of Florence’s camp?

sp.speaker: PAROLLES
sp.p: Upon my knowledge, he is, and lousy.

sp.speaker: FIRST LORD
sp.p: Nay, look not so upon me; we shall hear of your lordship anon.

sp.speaker: FIRST SOLDIER
sp.p: What is his reputation with the duke?

sp.speaker: PAROLLES
sp.p: The duke knows him for no other but a poor officer of mine, and writ to me this other day to turn him out o’ the band. I think I have his letter in my pocket.

sp.speaker: FIRST SOLDIER
sp.p: Marry, we’ll search.

sp.speaker: PAROLLES
sp.p: In good sadness, I do not know; either it is there or it is upon a file, with the duke’s other letters, in my tent.

sp.speaker: FIRST SOLDIER
sp.p: Here ’tis; here’s a paper; shall I read it to you?

sp.speaker: PAROLLES
sp.p: I do not know if it be it or no.

sp.speaker: BERTRAM
sp.p: Our interpreter does it well.

sp.speaker: FIRST LORD
sp.p: Excellently.

p.emph: Dian, the Count’s a fool, and full of gold.

sp.speaker: PAROLLES
sp.p: That is not the duke’s letter, sir; that is an advertisement to a proper maid in Florence, one Diana, to take heed of the allurement of one Count Rossillon, a foolish idle boy, but for all that very ruttish. I pray you, sir, put it up again.

sp.speaker: FIRST SOLDIER
sp.p: Nay, I’ll read it first by your favour.

sp.speaker: PAROLLES
sp.p: My meaning in’t, I protest, was very honest in the behalf of the maid; for I knew the young count to be a dangerous and lascivious boy, who is a whale to virginity, and devours up all the fry it finds.

sp.speaker: BERTRAM
sp.p: Damnable both sides rogue!

lg.l: When he swears oaths, bid him drop gold, and take it;
After he scores, he never pays the score.
Half won is match well made; match, and well make it;
He ne’er pays after-debts, take it before.
And say a soldier, ‘Dian,’ told thee this:
Men are to mell with, boys are not to kiss;
For count of this, the count’s a fool, I know it,
Who pays before, but not when he does owe it.
Thine, as he vow’d to thee in thine ear,
PAROLLES.

sp.speaker: BERTRAM
sp.p: He shall be whipped through the army with this rhyme in’s forehead.

sp.speaker: SECOND LORD
sp.p: This is your devoted friend, sir, the manifold linguist, and the armipotent soldier.

sp.speaker: BERTRAM
sp.p: I could endure anything before but a cat, and now he’s a cat to me.

sp.speaker: FIRST SOLDIER
sp.p: I perceive, sir, by our general’s looks we shall be fain to hang you.

sp.speaker: PAROLLES
sp.p: My life, sir, in any case. Not that I am afraid to die, but that, my offences being many, I would repent out the remainder of nature. Let me live, sir, in a dungeon, i’ the stocks, or anywhere, so I may live.

sp.speaker: FIRST SOLDIER
sp.p: We’ll see what may be done, so you confess freely. Therefore, once more to this Captain Dumaine: you have answer’d to his reputation with the duke, and to his valour. What is his honesty?

sp.speaker: PAROLLES
sp.p: He will steal, sir, an egg out of a cloister: for rapes and ravishments he parallels Nessus. He professes not keeping of oaths; in breaking them he is stronger than Hercules. He will lie, sir, with such volubility that you would think truth were a fool: drunkenness is his best virtue, for he will be swine-drunk, and in his sleep he does little harm, save to his bedclothes about him; but they know his conditions and lay him in straw. I have but little more to say, sir, of his honesty; he has everything that an honest man should not have; what an honest man should have, he has nothing.

sp.speaker: FIRST LORD
sp.p: I begin to love him for this.

sp.speaker: BERTRAM
sp.p: For this description of thine honesty? A pox upon him for me, he’s more and more a cat.

sp.speaker: FIRST SOLDIER
sp.p: What say you to his expertness in war?

sp.speaker: PAROLLES
sp.p: Faith, sir, has led the drum before the English tragedians,—to belie him I will not,—and more of his soldiership I know not, except in that country he had the honour to be the officer at a place there called Mile-end, to instruct for the doubling of files. I would do the man what honour I can, but of this I am not certain.

sp.speaker: FIRST LORD
sp.p: He hath out-villain’d villainy so far that the rarity redeems him.

sp.speaker: BERTRAM
sp.p: A pox on him! He’s a cat still.

sp.speaker: FIRST SOLDIER
sp.p: His qualities being at this poor price, I need not to ask you if gold will corrupt him to revolt.

sp.speaker: PAROLLES
sp.p: Sir, for a quart d’ecu he will sell the fee-simple of his salvation, the inheritance of it, and cut the entail from all remainders, and a perpetual succession for it perpetually.

sp.speaker: FIRST SOLDIER
sp.p: What’s his brother, the other Captain Dumaine?

sp.speaker: SECOND LORD
sp.p: Why does he ask him of me?

sp.speaker: FIRST SOLDIER
sp.p: What’s he?

sp.speaker: PAROLLES
sp.p: E’en a crow o’ the same nest; not altogether so great as the first in goodness, but greater a great deal in evil. He excels his brother for a coward, yet his brother is reputed one of the best that is. In a retreat he outruns any lackey; marry, in coming on he has the cramp.

sp.speaker: FIRST SOLDIER
sp.p: If your life be saved, will you undertake to betray the Florentine?

sp.speaker: PAROLLES
sp.p: Ay, and the captain of his horse, Count Rossillon.

sp.speaker: FIRST SOLDIER
sp.p: I’ll whisper with the general, and know his pleasure.

sp.speaker: PAROLLES
sp.p: Aside. I’ll no more drumming; a plague of all drums! Only to seem to deserve well, and to beguile the supposition of that lascivious young boy the count, have I run into this danger: yet who would have suspected an ambush where I was taken?

sp.speaker: FIRST SOLDIER
sp.p: There is no remedy, sir, but you must die. The general says you that have so traitorously discovered the secrets of your army, and made such pestiferous reports of men very nobly held, can serve the world for no honest use; therefore you must die. Come, headsman, off with his head.

sp.speaker: PAROLLES
sp.p: O Lord! sir, let me live, or let me see my death.

sp.speaker: FIRST SOLDIER
sp.p: That shall you, and take your leave of all your friends.

div.p: So, look about you; know you any here?

sp.speaker: BERTRAM
sp.p: Good morrow, noble captain.

sp.speaker: SECOND LORD
sp.p: God bless you, Captain Parolles.

sp.speaker: FIRST LORD
sp.p: God save you, noble captain.

sp.speaker: SECOND LORD
sp.p: Captain, what greeting will you to my Lord Lafew? I am for France.

sp.speaker: FIRST LORD
sp.p: Good Captain, will you give me a copy of the sonnet you writ to Diana in behalf of the Count Rossillon? And I were not a very coward I’d compel it of you; but fare you well.

sp.speaker: FIRST SOLDIER
sp.p: You are undone, captain: all but your scarf; that has a knot on’t yet.

sp.speaker: PAROLLES
sp.p: Who cannot be crushed with a plot?

sp.speaker: FIRST SOLDIER
sp.p: If you could find out a country where but women were that had received so much shame, you might begin an impudent nation. Fare ye well, sir. I am for France too; we shall speak of you there.

lg.l: Yet am I thankful. If my heart were great
’Twould burst at this. Captain I’ll be no more,
But I will eat, and drink, and sleep as soft
As captain shall. Simply the thing I am
Shall make me live. Who knows himself a braggart,
Let him fear this; for it will come to pass
That every braggart shall be found an ass.
Rust, sword; cool, blushes; and, Parolles live
Safest in shame; being fool’d, by foolery thrive.
There’s place and means for every man alive.
I’ll after them.

div.head: SCENE IV. Florence. A room in the Widow’s house.

lg.l: That you may well perceive I have not wrong’d you
One of the greatest in the Christian world
Shall be my surety; fore whose throne ’tis needful,
Ere I can perfect mine intents, to kneel.
Time was I did him a desired office,
Dear almost as his life; which gratitude
Through flinty Tartar’s bosom would peep forth,
And answer thanks. I duly am inform’d
His grace is at Marseilles; to which place
We have convenient convoy. You must know
I am supposed dead. The army breaking,
My husband hies him home, where, heaven aiding,
And by the leave of my good lord the king,
We’ll be before our welcome.
Gentle madam,
You never had a servant to whose trust
Your business was more welcome.
Nor you, mistress,
Ever a friend whose thoughts more truly labour
To recompense your love. Doubt not but heaven
Hath brought me up to be your daughter’s dower,
As it hath fated her to be my motive
And helper to a husband. But, O strange men!
That can such sweet use make of what they hate,
When saucy trusting of the cozen’d thoughts
Defiles the pitchy night; so lust doth play
With what it loathes, for that which is away.
But more of this hereafter. You, Diana,
Under my poor instructions yet must suffer
Something in my behalf.
Let death and honesty
Go with your impositions, I am yours
Upon your will to suffer.
Yet, I pray you;
But with the word the time will bring on summer,
When briers shall have leaves as well as thorns,
And be as sweet as sharp. We must away;
Our waggon is prepar’d, and time revives us.
All’s well that ends well; still the fine’s the crown.
Whate’er the course, the end is the renown.

div.head: SCENE V. Rossillon. A room in the Countess’s palace.

sp.speaker: LAFEW
sp.p: No, no, no, your son was misled with a snipt-taffeta fellow there, whose villanous saffron would have made all the unbak’d and doughy youth of a nation in his colour. Your daughter-in-law had been alive at this hour, and your son here at home, more advanc’d by the king than by that red-tail’d humble-bee I speak of.

sp.speaker: COUNTESS
sp.p: I would I had not known him; it was the death of the most virtuous gentlewoman that ever nature had praise for creating. If she had partaken of my flesh and cost me the dearest groans of a mother, I could not have owed her a more rooted love.

sp.speaker: LAFEW
sp.p: ’Twas a good lady, ’twas a good lady. We may pick a thousand salads ere we light on such another herb.

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: Indeed, sir, she was the sweet marjoram of the salad, or, rather, the herb of grace.

sp.speaker: LAFEW
sp.p: They are not herbs, you knave; they are nose-herbs.

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: I am no great Nebuchadnezzar, sir; I have not much skill in grass.

sp.speaker: LAFEW
sp.p: Whether dost thou profess thyself,—a knave or a fool?

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: A fool, sir, at a woman’s service, and a knave at a man’s.

sp.speaker: LAFEW
sp.p: Your distinction?

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: I would cozen the man of his wife, and do his service.

sp.speaker: LAFEW
sp.p: So you were a knave at his service indeed.

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: And I would give his wife my bauble, sir, to do her service.

sp.speaker: LAFEW
sp.p: I will subscribe for thee; thou art both knave and fool.

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: At your service.

sp.speaker: LAFEW
sp.p: No, no, no.

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: Why, sir, if I cannot serve you, I can serve as great a prince as you are.

sp.speaker: LAFEW
sp.p: Who’s that? a Frenchman?

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: Faith, sir, ’a has an English name; but his phisnomy is more hotter in France than there.

sp.speaker: LAFEW
sp.p: What prince is that?

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: The black prince, sir; alias the prince of darkness; alias the devil.

sp.speaker: LAFEW
sp.p: Hold thee, there’s my purse. I give thee not this to suggest thee from thy master thou talk’st of; serve him still.

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: I am a woodland fellow, sir, that always loved a great fire, and the master I speak of ever keeps a good fire. But sure he is the prince of the world; let his nobility remain in’s court. I am for the house with the narrow gate, which I take to be too little for pomp to enter: some that humble themselves may, but the many will be too chill and tender, and they’ll be for the flow’ry way that leads to the broad gate and the great fire.

sp.speaker: LAFEW
sp.p: Go thy ways, I begin to be a-weary of thee; and I tell thee so before, because I would not fall out with thee. Go thy ways; let my horses be well look’d to, without any tricks.

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: If I put any tricks upon ’em, sir, they shall be jades’ tricks, which are their own right by the law of nature.

sp.speaker: LAFEW
sp.p: A shrewd knave, and an unhappy.

sp.speaker: COUNTESS
sp.p: So he is. My lord that’s gone made himself much sport out of him; by his authority he remains here, which he thinks is a patent for his sauciness; and indeed he has no pace, but runs where he will.

sp.speaker: LAFEW
sp.p: I like him well; ’tis not amiss. And I was about to tell you, since I heard of the good lady’s death, and that my lord your son was upon his return home, I moved the king my master to speak in the behalf of my daughter; which, in the minority of them both, his majesty out of a self-gracious remembrance did first propose. His highness hath promis’d me to do it; and, to stop up the displeasure he hath conceived against your son, there is no fitter matter. How does your ladyship like it?

sp.speaker: COUNTESS
sp.p: With very much content, my lord, and I wish it happily effected.

sp.speaker: LAFEW
sp.p: His highness comes post from Marseilles, of as able body as when he number’d thirty; he will be here tomorrow, or I am deceived by him that in such intelligence hath seldom fail’d.

sp.speaker: COUNTESS
sp.p: It rejoices me that I hope I shall see him ere I die. I have letters that my son will be here tonight. I shall beseech your lordship to remain with me till they meet together.

sp.speaker: LAFEW
sp.p: Madam, I was thinking with what manners I might safely be admitted.

sp.speaker: COUNTESS
sp.p: You need but plead your honourable privilege.

sp.speaker: LAFEW
sp.p: Lady, of that I have made a bold charter; but, I thank my God, it holds yet.

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: O madam, yonder’s my lord your son with a patch of velvet on’s face; whether there be a scar under’t or no, the velvet knows; but ’tis a goodly patch of velvet. His left cheek is a cheek of two pile and a half, but his right cheek is worn bare.

sp.speaker: LAFEW
sp.p: A scar nobly got, or a noble scar, is a good livery of honour; so belike is that.

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: But it is your carbonado’d face.

sp.speaker: LAFEW
sp.p: Let us go see your son, I pray you. I long to talk with the young noble soldier.

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: Faith, there’s a dozen of ’em, with delicate fine hats, and most courteous feathers, which bow the head and nod at every man.

div.head: ACT V
SCENE I. Marseilles. A street.
div.stage: Enter Helena, Widow and Diana with two Attendants.

lg.l: But this exceeding posting day and night
Must wear your spirits low. We cannot help it.
But since you have made the days and nights as one,
To wear your gentle limbs in my affairs,
Be bold you do so grow in my requital
As nothing can unroot you. In happy time;—

div.p: This man may help me to his majesty’s ear, If he would spend his power. God save you, sir.

sp.speaker: GENTLEMAN
sp.p: And you.

sp.speaker: HELENA
sp.p: Sir, I have seen you in the court of France.

sp.speaker: GENTLEMAN
sp.p: I have been sometimes there.

lg.l: I do presume, sir, that you are not fallen
From the report that goes upon your goodness;
And therefore, goaded with most sharp occasions,
Which lay nice manners by, I put you to
The use of your own virtues, for the which
I shall continue thankful.

sp.speaker: GENTLEMAN
sp.p: What’s your will?

lg.l: That it will please you
To give this poor petition to the king,
And aid me with that store of power you have
To come into his presence.

sp.speaker: GENTLEMAN
sp.p: The king’s not here.

sp.speaker: HELENA
sp.p: Not here, sir?

lg.l: Not indeed.
He hence remov’d last night, and with more haste
Than is his use.

sp.speaker: WIDOW
sp.p: Lord, how we lose our pains!

lg.l: All’s well that ends well yet,
Though time seem so adverse and means unfit.
I do beseech you, whither is he gone?
Marry, as I take it, to Rossillon;
Whither I am going.
I do beseech you, sir,
Since you are like to see the king before me,
Commend the paper to his gracious hand,
Which I presume shall render you no blame,
But rather make you thank your pains for it.
I will come after you with what good speed
Our means will make us means.

sp.speaker: GENTLEMAN
sp.p: This I’ll do for you.

lg.l: And you shall find yourself to be well thank’d,
Whate’er falls more. We must to horse again.
Go, go, provide.

div.head: SCENE II. Rossillon. The inner court of the Countess’s palace.

sp.speaker: PAROLLES
sp.p: Good Monsieur Lavache, give my Lord Lafew this letter; I have ere now, sir, been better known to you, when I have held familiarity with fresher clothes; but I am now, sir, muddied in Fortune’s mood, and smell somewhat strong of her strong displeasure.

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: Truly, Fortune’s displeasure is but sluttish, if it smell so strongly as thou speak’st of. I will henceforth eat no fish of Fortune’s buttering. Pr’ythee, allow the wind.

sp.speaker: PAROLLES
sp.p: Nay, you need not to stop your nose, sir. I spake but by a metaphor.

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: Indeed, sir, if your metaphor stink, I will stop my nose, or against any man’s metaphor. Pr’ythee, get thee further.

sp.speaker: PAROLLES
sp.p: Pray you, sir, deliver me this paper.

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: Foh, pr’ythee stand away. A paper from Fortune’s close-stool to give to a nobleman! Look here he comes himself.

div.p: Here is a pur of Fortune’s, sir, or of Fortune’s cat, but not a musk-cat, that has fallen into the unclean fishpond of her displeasure, and as he says, is muddied withal. Pray you, sir, use the carp as you may, for he looks like a poor, decayed, ingenious, foolish, rascally knave. I do pity his distress in my similes of comfort, and leave him to your lordship.

sp.speaker: PAROLLES
sp.p: My lord, I am a man whom Fortune hath cruelly scratch’d.

sp.speaker: LAFEW
sp.p: And what would you have me to do? ’Tis too late to pare her nails now. Wherein have you played the knave with Fortune that she should scratch you, who of herself is a good lady, and would not have knaves thrive long under her? There’s a quart d’ecu for you. Let the justices make you and Fortune friends; I am for other business.

sp.speaker: PAROLLES
sp.p: I beseech your honour to hear me one single word.

sp.speaker: LAFEW
sp.p: You beg a single penny more. Come, you shall ha’t; save your word.

sp.speaker: PAROLLES
sp.p: My name, my good lord, is Parolles.

sp.speaker: LAFEW
sp.p: You beg more than word then. Cox my passion! Give me your hand. How does your drum?

sp.speaker: PAROLLES
sp.p: O my good lord, you were the first that found me.

sp.speaker: LAFEW
sp.p: Was I, in sooth? And I was the first that lost thee.

sp.speaker: PAROLLES
sp.p: It lies in you, my lord, to bring me in some grace, for you did bring me out.

sp.speaker: LAFEW
sp.p: Out upon thee, knave! dost thou put upon me at once both the office of God and the devil? One brings thee in grace, and the other brings thee out.

div.p: The king’s coming; I know by his trumpets. Sirrah, inquire further after me. I had talk of you last night; though you are a fool and a knave, you shall eat. Go to; follow.

sp.speaker: PAROLLES
sp.p: I praise God for you.

div.head: SCENE III. The same. A room in the Countess’s palace.
div.stage: Flourish. Enter King, Countess, Lafew, Lords, Gentlemen, Guards &c.

lg.l: We lost a jewel of her, and our esteem
Was made much poorer by it; but your son,
As mad in folly, lack’d the sense to know
Her estimation home.
’Tis past, my liege,
And I beseech your majesty to make it
Natural rebellion, done i’ the blaze of youth,
When oil and fire, too strong for reason’s force,
O’erbears it and burns on.
My honour’d lady,
I have forgiven and forgotten all,
Though my revenges were high bent upon him,
And watch’d the time to shoot.
This I must say,—
But first, I beg my pardon,—the young lord
Did to his majesty, his mother, and his lady,
Offence of mighty note; but to himself
The greatest wrong of all. He lost a wife
Whose beauty did astonish the survey
Of richest eyes; whose words all ears took captive;
Whose dear perfection hearts that scorn’d to serve
Humbly call’d mistress.
Praising what is lost
Makes the remembrance dear. Well, call him hither;
We are reconcil’d, and the first view shall kill
All repetition. Let him not ask our pardon;
The nature of his great offence is dead,
And deeper than oblivion do we bury
Th’ incensing relics of it. Let him approach
A stranger, no offender; and inform him
So ’tis our will he should.

sp.speaker: GENTLEMAN
sp.p: I shall, my liege.

sp.speaker: KING
sp.p: What says he to your daughter? Have you spoke?

sp.speaker: LAFEW
sp.p: All that he is hath reference to your highness.

lg.l: Then shall we have a match. I have letters sent me
That sets him high in fame.

sp.speaker: LAFEW
sp.p: He looks well on ’t.

lg.l: I am not a day of season,
For thou mayst see a sunshine and a hail
In me at once. But to the brightest beams
Distracted clouds give way; so stand thou forth;
The time is fair again.
My high-repented blames
Dear sovereign, pardon to me.
All is whole.
Not one word more of the consumed time.
Let’s take the instant by the forward top;
For we are old, and on our quick’st decrees
Th’inaudible and noiseless foot of time
Steals ere we can effect them. You remember
The daughter of this lord?
Admiringly, my liege. At first
I stuck my choice upon her, ere my heart
Durst make too bold herald of my tongue:
Where the impression of mine eye infixing,
Contempt his scornful perspective did lend me,
Which warp’d the line of every other favour,
Scorn’d a fair colour, or express’d it stolen,
Extended or contracted all proportions
To a most hideous object. Thence it came
That she whom all men prais’d, and whom myself,
Since I have lost, have lov’d, was in mine eye
The dust that did offend it.
Well excus’d:
That thou didst love her, strikes some scores away
From the great compt: but love that comes too late,
Like a remorseful pardon slowly carried,
To the great sender turns a sour offence,
Crying, That’s good that’s gone. Our rash faults
Make trivial price of serious things we have,
Not knowing them until we know their grave.
Oft our displeasures, to ourselves unjust,
Destroy our friends, and after weep their dust:
Our own love waking cries to see what’s done,
While shameful hate sleeps out the afternoon.
Be this sweet Helen’s knell, and now forget her.
Send forth your amorous token for fair Maudlin.
The main consents are had, and here we’ll stay
To see our widower’s second marriage-day.
Which better than the first, O dear heaven, bless!
Or, ere they meet, in me, O nature, cesse!
Come on, my son, in whom my house’s name
Must be digested; give a favour from you,
To sparkle in the spirits of my daughter,
That she may quickly come.

div.stage: Bertram gives a ring to Lafew.
div.p: By my old beard, And ev’ry hair that’s on ’t, Helen that’s dead Was a sweet creature: such a ring as this, The last that e’er I took her leave at court, I saw upon her finger.

sp.speaker: BERTRAM
sp.p: Hers it was not.

lg.l: Now, pray you, let me see it; for mine eye,
While I was speaking, oft was fasten’d to it.
This ring was mine; and when I gave it Helen
I bade her, if her fortunes ever stood
Necessitied to help, that by this token
I would relieve her. Had you that craft to ’reave her
Of what should stead her most?
My gracious sovereign,
Howe’er it pleases you to take it so,
The ring was never hers.
Son, on my life,
I have seen her wear it; and she reckon’d it
At her life’s rate.

sp.speaker: LAFEW
sp.p: I am sure I saw her wear it.

lg.l: You are deceiv’d, my lord; she never saw it.
In Florence was it from a casement thrown me,
Wrapp’d in a paper, which contain’d the name
Of her that threw it. Noble she was, and thought
I stood engag’d; but when I had subscrib’d
To mine own fortune, and inform’d her fully
I could not answer in that course of honour
As she had made the overture, she ceas’d,
In heavy satisfaction, and would never
Receive the ring again.
Plutus himself,
That knows the tinct and multiplying medicine,
Hath not in nature’s mystery more science
Than I have in this ring. ’Twas mine, ’twas Helen’s,
Whoever gave it you. Then if you know
That you are well acquainted with yourself,
Confess ’twas hers, and by what rough enforcement
You got it from her. She call’d the saints to surety
That she would never put it from her finger
Unless she gave it to yourself in bed,
Where you have never come, or sent it us
Upon her great disaster.

sp.speaker: BERTRAM
sp.p: She never saw it.

lg.l: Thou speak’st it falsely, as I love mine honour,
And mak’st conjectural fears to come into me
Which I would fain shut out. If it should prove
That thou art so inhuman,—’twill not prove so:
And yet I know not, thou didst hate her deadly.
And she is dead; which nothing but to close
Her eyes myself, could win me to believe
More than to see this ring. Take him away.

div.p: My fore-past proofs, howe’er the matter fall, Shall tax my fears of little vanity, Having vainly fear’d too little. Away with him. We’ll sift this matter further.

lg.l: If you shall prove
This ring was ever hers, you shall as easy
Prove that I husbanded her bed in Florence,
Where she yet never was.

sp.speaker: KING
sp.p: I am wrapp’d in dismal thinkings.

lg.l: Gracious sovereign,
Whether I have been to blame or no, I know not:
Here’s a petition from a Florentine,
Who hath for four or five removes come short
To tender it herself. I undertook it,
Vanquish’d thereto by the fair grace and speech
Of the poor suppliant, who by this, I know,
Is here attending: her business looks in her
With an importing visage, and she told me
In a sweet verbal brief, it did concern
Your highness with herself.

l.emph: Upon his many protestations to marry me when his wife was dead, I blush to say it, he won me. Now is the Count Rossillon a widower; his vows are forfeited to me, and my honour’s paid to him. He stole from Florence, taking no leave, and I follow him to his country for justice. Grant it me, O king, in you it best lies; otherwise a seducer flourishes, and a poor maid is undone.

lg.l: DIANA CAPILET.

sp.speaker: LAFEW
sp.p: I will buy me a son-in-law in a fair, and toll for this. I’ll none of him.

lg.l: The heavens have thought well on thee, Lafew,
To bring forth this discovery. Seek these suitors.
Go speedily, and bring again the count.

div.p: I am afeard the life of Helen, lady, Was foully snatch’d.

sp.speaker: COUNTESS
sp.p: Now, justice on the doers!

lg.l: I wonder, sir, since wives are monsters to you,
And that you fly them as you swear them lordship,
Yet you desire to marry. What woman’s that?
I am, my lord, a wretched Florentine,
Derived from the ancient Capilet;
My suit, as I do understand, you know,
And therefore know how far I may be pitied.
I am her mother, sir, whose age and honour
Both suffer under this complaint we bring,
And both shall cease, without your remedy.

sp.speaker: KING
sp.p: Come hither, count; do you know these women?

lg.l: My lord, I neither can nor will deny
But that I know them. Do they charge me further?

sp.speaker: DIANA
sp.p: Why do you look so strange upon your wife?

sp.speaker: BERTRAM
sp.p: She’s none of mine, my lord.

lg.l: If you shall marry,
You give away this hand, and that is mine,
You give away heaven’s vows, and those are mine,
You give away myself, which is known mine;
For I by vow am so embodied yours
That she which marries you must marry me,
Either both or none.

sp.speaker: LAFEW
sp.p: To Bertram Your reputation comes too short for my daughter; you are no husband for her.

lg.l: My lord, this is a fond and desperate creature
Whom sometime I have laugh’d with. Let your highness
Lay a more noble thought upon mine honour
Than for to think that I would sink it here.
Sir, for my thoughts, you have them ill to friend
Till your deeds gain them; fairer prove your honour
Than in my thought it lies!
Good my lord,
Ask him upon his oath, if he does think
He had not my virginity.

sp.speaker: KING
sp.p: What say’st thou to her?

lg.l: She’s impudent, my lord,
And was a common gamester to the camp.
He does me wrong, my lord; if I were so
He might have bought me at a common price.
Do not believe him. O, behold this ring,
Whose high respect and rich validity
Did lack a parallel; yet for all that
He gave it to a commoner o’ the camp,
If I be one.
He blushes, and ’tis it.
Of six preceding ancestors, that gem
Conferr’d by testament to th’ sequent issue,
Hath it been owed and worn. This is his wife;
That ring’s a thousand proofs.
Methought you said
You saw one here in court could witness it.
I did, my lord, but loath am to produce
So bad an instrument; his name’s Parolles.

sp.speaker: LAFEW
sp.p: I saw the man today, if man he be.

sp.speaker: KING
sp.p: Find him, and bring him hither.

lg.l: What of him?
He’s quoted for a most perfidious slave,
With all the spots o’ the world tax’d and debauch’d:
Whose nature sickens but to speak a truth.
Am I or that or this for what he’ll utter,
That will speak anything?

sp.speaker: KING
sp.p: She hath that ring of yours.

lg.l: I think she has. Certain it is I lik’d her
And boarded her i’ the wanton way of youth.
She knew her distance, and did angle for me,
Madding my eagerness with her restraint,
As all impediments in fancy’s course
Are motives of more fancy; and in fine,
Her infinite cunning with her modern grace,
Subdu’d me to her rate; she got the ring,
And I had that which any inferior might
At market-price have bought.
I must be patient.
You that have turn’d off a first so noble wife
May justly diet me. I pray you yet,—
Since you lack virtue, I will lose a husband—
Send for your ring, I will return it home,
And give me mine again.

sp.speaker: BERTRAM
sp.p: I have it not.

sp.speaker: KING
sp.p: What ring was yours, I pray you?

lg.l: Sir, much like
The same upon your finger.

sp.speaker: KING
sp.p: Know you this ring? This ring was his of late.

sp.speaker: DIANA
sp.p: And this was it I gave him, being abed.

lg.l: The story then goes false you threw it him
Out of a casement.

sp.speaker: DIANA
sp.p: I have spoke the truth.

sp.speaker: BERTRAM
sp.p: My lord, I do confess the ring was hers.

lg.l: You boggle shrewdly; every feather starts you.
Is this the man you speak of?

sp.speaker: DIANA
sp.p: Ay, my lord.

lg.l: Tell me, sirrah, but tell me true I charge you,
Not fearing the displeasure of your master,
Which on your just proceeding, I’ll keep off,—
By him and by this woman here what know you?

sp.speaker: PAROLLES
sp.p: So please your majesty, my master hath been an honourable gentleman. Tricks he hath had in him, which gentlemen have.

sp.speaker: KING
sp.p: Come, come, to the purpose. Did he love this woman?

sp.speaker: PAROLLES
sp.p: Faith, sir, he did love her; but how?

sp.speaker: KING
sp.p: How, I pray you?

sp.speaker: PAROLLES
sp.p: He did love her, sir, as a gentleman loves a woman.

sp.speaker: KING
sp.p: How is that?

sp.speaker: PAROLLES
sp.p: He lov’d her, sir, and lov’d her not.

lg.l: As thou art a knave and no knave.
What an equivocal companion is this!

sp.speaker: PAROLLES
sp.p: I am a poor man, and at your majesty’s command.

sp.speaker: LAFEW
sp.p: He’s a good drum, my lord, but a naughty orator.

sp.speaker: DIANA
sp.p: Do you know he promised me marriage?

sp.speaker: PAROLLES
sp.p: Faith, I know more than I’ll speak.

sp.speaker: KING
sp.p: But wilt thou not speak all thou know’st?

sp.speaker: PAROLLES
sp.p: Yes, so please your majesty. I did go between them as I said; but more than that, he loved her, for indeed he was mad for her, and talked of Satan, and of Limbo, and of furies, and I know not what: yet I was in that credit with them at that time that I knew of their going to bed; and of other motions, as promising her marriage, and things which would derive me ill will to speak of; therefore I will not speak what I know.

sp.speaker: KING
sp.p: Thou hast spoken all already, unless thou canst say they are married; but thou art too fine in thy evidence; therefore stand aside. This ring, you say, was yours?

sp.speaker: DIANA
sp.p: Ay, my good lord.

sp.speaker: KING
sp.p: Where did you buy it? Or who gave it you?

sp.speaker: DIANA
sp.p: It was not given me, nor I did not buy it.

sp.speaker: KING
sp.p: Who lent it you?

sp.speaker: DIANA
sp.p: It was not lent me neither.

sp.speaker: KING
sp.p: Where did you find it then?

sp.speaker: DIANA
sp.p: I found it not.

lg.l: If it were yours by none of all these ways,
How could you give it him?

sp.speaker: DIANA
sp.p: I never gave it him.

sp.speaker: LAFEW
sp.p: This woman’s an easy glove, my lord; she goes off and on at pleasure.

sp.speaker: KING
sp.p: This ring was mine, I gave it his first wife.

sp.speaker: DIANA
sp.p: It might be yours or hers for ought I know.

lg.l: Take her away, I do not like her now.
To prison with her. And away with him.
Unless thou tell’st me where thou hadst this ring,
Thou diest within this hour.

sp.speaker: DIANA
sp.p: I’ll never tell you.

sp.speaker: KING
sp.p: Take her away.

sp.speaker: DIANA
sp.p: I’ll put in bail, my liege.

sp.speaker: KING
sp.p: I think thee now some common customer.

sp.speaker: DIANA
sp.p: By Jove, if ever I knew man, ’twas you.

sp.speaker: KING
sp.p: Wherefore hast thou accus’d him all this while?

lg.l: Because he’s guilty, and he is not guilty.
He knows I am no maid, and he’ll swear to’t:
I’ll swear I am a maid, and he knows not.
Great King, I am no strumpet, by my life;
I am either maid, or else this old man’s wife.

sp.speaker: KING
sp.p: She does abuse our ears; to prison with her.

sp.speaker: DIANA
sp.p: Good mother, fetch my bail. Stay, royal sir;

div.p: The jeweller that owes the ring is sent for, And he shall surety me. But for this lord Who hath abus’d me as he knows himself, Though yet he never harm’d me, here I quit him. He knows himself my bed he hath defil’d; And at that time he got his wife with child. Dead though she be, she feels her young one kick; So there’s my riddle: one that’s dead is quick, And now behold the meaning.

lg.l: Is there no exorcist
Beguiles the truer office of mine eyes?
Is’t real that I see?
No, my good lord;
’Tis but the shadow of a wife you see,
The name, and not the thing.

sp.speaker: BERTRAM
sp.p: Both, both. O, pardon!

lg.l: O, my good lord, when I was like this maid;
I found you wondrous kind. There is your ring,
And, look you, here’s your letter. This it says,
‘When from my finger you can get this ring,
And is by me with child, &c.’ This is done;
Will you be mine now you are doubly won?
If she, my liege, can make me know this clearly,
I’ll love her dearly, ever, ever dearly.
If it appear not plain, and prove untrue,
Deadly divorce step between me and you!
O my dear mother, do I see you living?
Mine eyes smell onions; I shall weep anon.
to Parolles Good Tom Drum, lend me a handkercher.
So, I thank thee. Wait on me home, I’ll make sport with thee.
Let thy courtesies alone, they are scurvy ones.
Let us from point to point this story know,
To make the even truth in pleasure flow.
To Diana. If thou beest yet a fresh uncropped flower,
Choose thou thy husband, and I’ll pay thy dower;
For I can guess that by thy honest aid,
Thou kept’st a wife herself, thyself a maid.
Of that and all the progress more and less,
Resolvedly more leisure shall express.
All yet seems well, and if it end so meet,
The bitter past, more welcome is the sweet.

p.emph: The king’s a beggar, now the play is done; All is well ended if this suit be won, That you express content; which we will pay With strife to please you, day exceeding day. Ours be your patience then, and yours our parts; Your gentle hands lend us, and take our hearts.
